task: Write one sentence of your own using the word injunction. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know injunction should be able to work it out from your sentence.

A request politely asks someone to stop an activity, while an injunction legally compels them to stop.
An injunction usually pauses an activity while a case is decided, while a permanent ban ends the activity for good.

A court order is any official command a judge issues — to pay damages or hand over documents. An injunction is one specific kind of court order: it requires a party to do something or, more often, to stop doing it, usually while a case is decided. Every injunction is a court order; most court orders are not injunctions.

A prohibition is an order forbidding an action, and it can come from any authority — a legislature, an agency, a landlord — as a standing rule. An injunction comes only from a court, binds the specific parties in a live dispute, and usually lasts until the case ends. A prohibition sets a standing rule; an injunction polices one dispute.

For months, the residents of Milbrook watched gray foam drift down the river behind the chemical plant.
Independent tests showed the plant was releasing waste far above legal limits.
The town sued, and the judge granted an injunction ordering the plant to halt all discharges immediately.
Until the case is resolved, the plant cannot release a single gallon into the river.
The court order forcing the plant to stop its discharges is an injunction, a legal command to stop a specific action.
Injunction appears almost exclusively in legal contexts, usually with verbs like issue, grant, or seek.
Courts most often use injunctions to stop an activity temporarily while a lawsuit is being decided.

The gravel quarry on the ridge had blasted twice a week for years, and the village below had learned to live with the rattle of its windows.
When cracks began climbing the walls of the century-old schoolhouse, the village sued, arguing the shocks were tearing the building apart.
A trial on the evidence could take two years, and the school could not wait that long for relief.
So the villagers asked the court for an injunction, and the judge granted it: all blasting must stop while the lawsuit runs its course.
The quarry still operates its crushers and trucks, and if it wins at trial the blasting may resume — but until then, the ridge stays quiet.
